Oh, sleep... sleep is just a complete disaster right now. I mean, you would think that after chasing five-year-olds around a classroom all day, managing meltdowns and tying shoes, I would just hit the pillow and completely pass out, right? That’s what people assume. But it is the exact opposite.

I'll spend hours, literally hours, just staring at the ceiling, replaying the most random or stressful things. I'll go over old interview answers from years ago, agonizing over whether I sounded foolish, or I'll start mentally tallying up our household bills, trying to calculate if the electric bill is going to be higher this month and how that affects the budget. And the paperwork—don't even get me started on the state licensing forms for the classroom. Those are a nightmare on their own. I'll lie there in bed panicking over whether I checked the right boxes on the safety compliance sheets or if the fire drill log was signed properly by the administration. It just loops and loops in my head.

And the worst part is, even when my body finally just gives out and I do manage to sleep, it doesn't last. I almost always wake up around four in the morning. And I don't just wake up peacefully, you know, slowly drifting awake. I wake up already completely tense—my neck and shoulders are already locked up again—and I am immediately calculating every single thing that could possibly go wrong that day. It's 4:00 AM, pitch black outside, and I'm lying there stressing about what happens if a parent gets upset about a scraped knee on the playground, or what if I lose control of the transition to art time. By the time my actual alarm goes off at six, I feel like I've already lived a full, stressful day. It's just... I'm so tired.

Sudden? Like, out of nowhere? Um... no. No, I... I really wouldn't say that. I know some people get that, right? Where they're just walking down the street or at the grocery store and suddenly they feel terrified out of the blue, and it hits them all at once like a wave. I’m just always up there, always bracing, always waiting for the other shoe to drop, whether I'm cutting out construction paper shapes for the kids or just trying to eat my dinner at home. It never peaks and then fades. So, no, not a sudden episode. Just this... endless, exhausting plateau of worry. Does that make sense? Oh, it’s... it’s really everywhere. I mean, it certainly anchors itself around teaching because that's my life, that's what I do, but it doesn't stay there. It branches out like... well, like ivy, you know? It just creeps in and takes over everything else. It’s never just a simple, isolated thought of 'I hope I get a job.' 

My mind just keeps circling and circling in this endless, exhausting loop. I’ll be lying in bed, and first I'm agonizing over whether I'll ever get hired again, like we were just talking about with those applications and the frozen feeling. But then, almost immediately, that thought morphs into this intense panic about my past interactions. I'll start obsessing over whether I've somehow ruined my reputation with the parents in the district. You know how small these school communities can be—parents talk at the playground, they have their little group chats and email chains, and I'll convince myself that I said something slightly awkward during a drop-off two years ago, and now they all think I'm incompetent and I'm secretly blacklisted from every school in the county. 

And then, because I'm only doing that piecemeal substitute work, the financial panic sets in. I'm fifty-three now, so it’s not like I have decades and decades to bounce back and rebuild my savings. I'll start obsessively calculating my pension contributions in my head at two in the morning, worrying whether retirement is just completely slipping away from me. I'll picture myself at seventy, unable to pay my rent or afford groceries, all because I can't get my act together and secure a lead teacher spot right now. It just spirals into this massive dread about my entire future. 

But I think the worst part, the part that really breaks my heart, is how it attacks my actual ability to be around the kids. I'll think about a tiny, insignificant thing—like a small mistake I made during a story-time activity, maybe I stumbled over a word or I didn't transition them to the sensory table perfectly smoothly—and my brain will just run away with it. I'll actually start convincing myself that a mistake like that means I shouldn't be trusted with children anymore. That maybe I'm losing my touch, or I'm somehow a detriment to their early development. Which is ridiculous, right? I know it's ridiculous, I have a master's degree, I've been doing this for years! But the worry doesn't care about my degree. It just jumps from my career, to my reputation, to my financial survival, to my fundamental worth as an educator, over and over and over. 

So, to answer your question, no, it's definitely not just about the immediate tasks of teaching. It's... it's this massive web that just catches absolutely everything in my life. I don't know how to turn it off.

Oh, absolutely. It ruins them. It really does. Take my garden, for example. I have this little vegetable patch behind my place—I usually do heirloom tomatoes, some zucchini, a really nice trellis with runner beans. I used to love getting out there on a weekend. But the second I'm out there, my mind just starts up. I try so hard to stop it, I really do. I try telling myself, you know, "Just make a mental list of what you need to do tomorrow and be done with it," or I'll try to just say a quick prayer to calm my nerves, or I'll tell myself, "Just weed this one section of the tomato bed, just focus on the next practical step right in front of you." I really try to force myself to just be present and pull the dandelions. 

But... it’s like my brain just won't let me. It doesn't matter what I do. One worry just hands off to another, like some kind of exhausting relay race. I'll start worrying about an interview, and then that instantly turns into worrying about my savings, and then that turns into worrying about whether I left a window open at the apartment. It just cascades. And before I know it, I'm just kneeling there in the dirt, completely frozen, and I've lost half the afternoon to it. 

I'll look at my watch and three hours have gone by, and I haven't actually enjoyed a single second of being outside. I haven't even finished weeding the one row! It's just so incredibly frustrating because I want to enjoy my life, I want to enjoy the things that used to bring me peace, but I just cannot control where my mind goes. It just hijacks my whole day, no matter how hard I try to distract myself with the things I'm supposed to love doing.

I'll lie there in bed panicking over whether I checked the right boxes on the safety compliance sheets or if the fire drill log was signed properly by the administration. It just loops and loops in my head.\n\nAnd the worst part is, even when my body finally just gives out and I do manage to sleep, it doesn't last. I almost always wake up around four in the morning. And I don't just wake up peacefully, you know, slowly drifting awake. I wake up already completely tense—my neck and shoulders are already locked up again—and I am immediately calculating every single thing that could possibly go wrong that day. It's 4:00 AM, pitch black outside, and I'm lying there stressing about what happens if a parent gets upset about a scraped knee on the playground, or what if I lose control of the transition to art time. By the time my actual alarm goes off at six, I feel like I've already lived a full, stressful day. It's just... I'm so tired.\n\nDoctor: Are you experiencing any feelings of sadness or hopelessness?\n\nPatient: Sadness? Um, no... no, I really wouldn't say that. I mean, I know sometimes people think that when you're this exhausted and run down, you must be, you know, depressed or down in the dumps, but it’s really not like that for me at all. It’s not a heavy, dark cloud kind of feeling. I definitely don't feel like giving up. \n\nI actually still really love my life, and I still absolutely love teaching. I've got my master's in early childhood education, I'm 53 years old, so I've been doing this for quite a while, and I still get a real kick out of the kids. Just yesterday, one of my boys, little Leo, finally figured out how to hold his safety scissors the right way without getting his thumb stuck, and I was just thrilled! So the joy is definitely still there. I'm not hopeless at all. \n\nIt’s just... instead of feeling low or empty, I feel completely over-full, if that makes sense? Like a cup that's just overflowing with electricity. I'm honestly too wired, too keyed up to be sad. It’s a very high-energy kind of misery. If I ever feel like crying, it's strictly out of pure frustration because I just want my brain to stop spinning for five minutes so I can rest. But it's never because I feel hopeless about the future. I just feel... terrified of it, I guess? Or at least terrified of all the tiny, microscopic things that could potentially go wrong in the next twenty-four hours. So, no, not sad. Um, headaches or stomach things? You know, no, not really. I've actually never been much of a headache person, thankfully. My mother, she used to get these absolutely terrible migraines when I was growing up—the kind where she’d have to lie down in a completely dark room with a cold washcloth over her eyes for two days straight, and we all had to tiptoe around the house so we wouldn't disturb her. So my stomach handles everything just fine. Sometimes I might forget to eat lunch entirely because I'm so wrapped up in worrying about my savings or analyzing an interaction I had with the principal three weeks ago, but when I do finally sit down to eat, it doesn't upset my stomach at all. 

So, no, I wouldn't say I have any gastrointestinal issues or headaches. It really just comes back to that muscle tension you brought up. That’s where it all lives physically for me. It’s like my shoulders are practically glued to my earlobes by the end of the day, and my jaw is just clamped shut from bracing myself against my own thoughts, but... yeah, no stomach aches or head pain. Just the tension and the endless, exhausting worrying.

I’m just always up there, always bracing, always waiting for the other shoe to drop, whether I'm cutting out construction paper shapes for the kids or just trying to eat my dinner at home. It never peaks and then fades. So, no, not a sudden episode. Just this... endless, exhausting plateau of worry. Does that make sense? Because I definitely don't get those quick, intense episodes you're talking about, it's just always running in the background.\n\nDoctor: Are you finding it difficult to perform your daily tasks or responsibilities as a kindergarten teacher due to the way you've been feeling?\n\nPatient: Well, it’s... it’s actually become a huge problem. And then, on the rare occasions I actually do get all the paperwork in and they call me in, I’ve completely stumbled through the interviews. I had one two weeks ago, and they asked me a completely standard question about managing transition times, and my brain just flooded with every worst-case scenario. I ended up rambling, losing my train of thought, and I could just see the principal looking at me with this polite, confused smile. I will spend three days agonizing over whether the book is too long, if the kids will get restless and start acting out, or if I haven't tied it into the curriculum perfectly enough. It’s exhausting. \n\nSo, honestly, this whole thing... it’s keeping me from getting back into the classroom in any reliable way. I have my master's degree, I have years of experience, I know how to teach! Well, outside of the actual act of teaching itself... yes, absolutely, because it's completely paralyzed my ability to manage my daily life and, ironically, to get back to teaching. I mean, just the sheer logistics of my life are falling apart right now.

I had one a few weeks ago at a really lovely little magnet school, and the principal asked me a basic question about lesson planning—something I could literally answer in my sleep! But my mind was just racing, worrying about what they were thinking, whether they could tell I was anxious, if they thought I was too old for the role... and I just babbled. I stumbled over my words so badly. I could see them looking at me, and I just knew I was ruining it in real-time, but I couldn't stop.

It’s even bleeding into my community stuff, things that used to just be purely for fun. I used to love doing the weekend story-time at the public library. I told the head librarian I can only be a backup reader now. 

So, really, this whole thing... the anxiety is just keeping me from getting back into the classroom in any reliable way. It’s dictating everything I do, or rather, everything I can't do anymore. It's just so frustrating to watch yourself fail at basic steps and not be able to stop it.

========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Well, it's funny you ask if there's a particular theme, because honestly, it feels like it's just a giant web of everything, but I suppose if I really step back and look at it, it all centers around my career, my standing, and just... my entire future. 

I'll just sit in my armchair for hours, staring out the window, and my mind just keeps circling and circling about whether I'll ever get hired again. I mean, I'm fifty-three years old with a master's degree. I'm not exactly a twenty-two-year-old fresh out of college who they can pay the absolute base salary. I constantly worry that districts are looking at my resume and just seeing a liability, or someone who costs too much, and I just obsess over the idea that my days in the classroom are permanently over. 

And then, of course, that instantly spirals into this massive panic about my reputation. I have spent decades building trust in this community. Decades. But lately, I am constantly agonizing over whether I've completely ruined my reputation with the parents. You know how parents are these days—they talk, they have these neighborhood Facebook groups and group texts, and I just convince myself that they're all whispering about me. I worry they think I've lost my touch, or that I'm unreliable now because I'm not teaching full-time. I'll analyze a five-minute conversation I had with a former student's mother at the grocery store for three weeks, completely terrified that I said something wrong.

Which, naturally, leads right into the financial terror of it all. Because if I can't get hired, and my reputation is ruined, then I start doing the math in my head, just obsessively worrying about whether my retirement is slipping away. I had a very specific plan, you know? A timeline for my state pension and my savings, and now I feel like I'm just watching it all evaporate right in front of my eyes because I can't get myself together to secure a new position. 

But I think the most exhausting part, the part that really shows how ridiculous my brain is being, is how I agonize over the absolute tiniest things. Like I mentioned that library story-time earlier? I'll make one tiny, insignificant mistake—maybe I accidentally skip a page in a picture book, or I stumble over the words in a little finger-play song—and my brain will just latch onto it like a vice. I will spend days completely convinced that this one small mistake in a volunteer story-time activity means I am fundamentally incompetent and shouldn't even be trusted with children anymore. It's like my mind takes this massive, illogical leap from a skipped page to "you are a fraud and a danger to the profession." It just keeps circling these exact same fears, over and over, and I can't seem to find the off switch.

Activities... well, yes. It's actually the main reason I finally made the appointment to see you. I've always been a big music person. And instead of just filling out the forms like a capable adult, I just stare at the screen. I get so overwhelmed by the 'what ifs' and the dread that I've actually missed application deadlines. Several of them, actually. Good positions, too, but I just let the clock run out on the deadline because I was too paralyzed by the worry to just hit submit. \n\nAnd then, on the rare occasions when I do force myself to follow through and I actually get a call back, I've just completely stumbled through interviews. I had one a few weeks ago at a really lovely little magnet school, and the principal asked me a basic question about lesson planning—something I could literally answer in my sleep! But my mind was just racing, worrying about what they were thinking, whether they could tell I was anxious, if they thought I was too old for the role... and I just babbled. I stumbled over my words so badly. I could see them looking at me, and I just knew I was ruining it in real-time, but I couldn't stop.\n\nIt’s even bleeding into my community stuff, things that used to just be purely for fun. I used to love doing the weekend story-time at the public library. It was wonderful, just me and the kids and a big stack of picture books. But lately... I've stopped volunteering for story-time entirely, unless someone else handles all the planning. I just can't bear the weight of organizing it myself anymore, the fear of messing it up or choosing the wrong book or losing the kids' attention is just too heavy. I told the head librarian I can only be a backup reader now. \n\nSo, really, this whole thing... the anxiety is just keeping me from getting back into the classroom in any reliable way. It’s dictating everything I do, or rather, everything I can't do anymore. It's just so frustrating to watch yourself fail at basic steps and not be able to stop it.\n\nDoctor: Is there a particular theme or topic that your worries most often center around?\n\nPatient: Well, it's funny you ask if there's a particular theme, because honestly, it feels like it's just a giant web of everything, but I suppose if I really step back and look at it, it all centers around my career, my standing, and just... my entire future. \n\nI'll just sit in my armchair for hours, staring out the window, and my mind just keeps circling and circling about whether I'll ever get hired again. I mean, I'm fifty-three years old with a master's degree. I'm not exactly a twenty-two-year-old fresh out of college who they can pay the absolute base salary. I constantly worry that districts are looking at my resume and just seeing a liability, or someone who costs too much, and I just obsess over the idea that my days in the classroom are permanently over. \n\nAnd then, of course, that instantly spirals into this massive panic about my reputation. I have spent decades building trust in this community. Decades. But lately, I am constantly agonizing over whether I've completely ruined my reputation with the parents. You know how parents are these days—they talk, they have these neighborhood Facebook groups and group texts, and I just convince myself that they're all whispering about me. I worry they think I've lost my touch, or that I'm unreliable now because I'm not teaching full-time. I'll analyze a five-minute conversation I had with a former student's mother at the grocery store for three weeks, completely terrified that I said something wrong.\n\nWhich, naturally, leads right into the financial terror of it all. Because if I can't get hired, and my reputation is ruined, then I start doing the math in my head, just obsessively worrying about whether my retirement is slipping away. I had a very specific plan, you know? A timeline for my state pension and my savings, and now I feel like I'm just watching it all evaporate right in front of my eyes because I can't get myself together to secure a new position. \n\nBut I think the most exhausting part, the part that really shows how ridiculous my brain is being, is how I agonize over the absolute tiniest things. Like I mentioned that library story-time earlier? I'll make one tiny, insignificant mistake—maybe I accidentally skip a page in a picture book, or I stumble over the words in a little finger-play song—and my brain will just latch onto it like a vice. I will spend days completely convinced that this one small mistake in a volunteer story-time activity means I am fundamentally incompetent and shouldn't even be trusted with children anymore. It's like my mind takes this massive, illogical leap from a skipped page to \"you are a fraud and a danger to the profession.\" It just keeps circling these exact same fears, over and over, and I can't seem to find the off switch.\n\nDoctor: Are you finding it difficult to connect with others or maintain social relationships due to your constant worrying?\n\nPatient: Social relationships... you know, connecting with people? I... actually, I wouldn't say that's an issue for me, surprisingly enough. I mean, you'd think it would be, with how much space this worry takes up in my head, but no, I still have my friends. Intimacy... well, I suppose that goes back to what I was saying earlier about my friends and my sister. I don't think I'm losing that connection, no. I mean, my wife, Sarah—we've been married for nearly thirty years now, since right after I started teaching, actually. And she's... she's just a saint, really. She sees how wound up I am, how I'm just pacing the house at night, worrying about our retirement accounts and whether I'm going to get hired anywhere else. 

And she doesn't pull away. If anything, she tries to pull me closer. She'll sit with me on the couch while I'm just obsessing over some minor detail of my resume, and she'll just hold my hand. My hands are usually freezing cold these days, just from the stress of it all, I think, but she just holds them. So the connection is there. The intimacy is there. 

But... I will say, I feel incredibly guilty about it. Because I know I'm not fully present. I walked out of there knowing I didn't get the job before I even reached my car.\n\nIt's even ruining the things I do for fun, like the Saturday morning story-time at the community library. I used to love doing that, bringing in the felt boards and doing all the voices for the kids. But I've completely stopped volunteering for it. The only way I can even participate now is if one of the librarians handles all the planning and just points me to a chair and hands me a book. One worry just hands off to another, like some terrible relay race in my mind, and it just keeps going and going. \n\nAnd before I know it, the trowel is still sitting in the dirt, I haven't pulled a single weed, I haven't written anything on my list, and I look at my watch and I've literally lost half the afternoon to it.
